According to the Joint Commission's 2018 Sentinel Event Alert, establishing trust is essential in improving patient safety reporting. Team members who feel emotionally at ease at work tend to communicate more freely about potential patient safety issues. If trust is present within the team, people will be more likely to report potential safety issues, near misses, or events as they'll feel their input will be taken seriously.  

### Why is it important?

When a team member feels guarded or afraid to speak up, he or she may be less open and collaborative, and experience anxieties that prohibit them from reporting safety concerns for fear of retribution. **Below are some tips for creating a high-trust culture for safety:**

##### Build Empathy

Share your experiences and aspirations with your team, and create opportunities for them to share with each other. This might mean spotlighting a different team member during scheduled huddles and asking them to share a bit about themselves. Knowing what your teammates are going through, where they're coming from, and what they value is fundamental to building trust.

##### Focus on Positives

In team discussions, make a habit of emphasizing growth, progress, and moving forward. For example, when safety protocol mistakes happen focus more on next steps rather than dwelling on the misstep. Be sure that employee suggestions (i.e. related or unrelated to safety) or other "speaking upâ€ behaviors are recognized as positives as this should lead to increased safety reporting behaviors.  

##### Detect Issues Early

If you see an issue with a team member, try to solve it right away. If you wait, it could become a bigger issue. 

##### Don't Belittle or Place Blame

By being clear that it is not acceptable for team members to treat each other unkindly, you ensure that the team feels comfortable and secure.  Don't let them point fingers. This lowers morale, undermines trust, and is ultimately unproductive. Instead, encourage everyone in your group to think about the mistake in a constructive way and learn from it. What can you all do to fix what happened, and move forward together? 

##### Lead by Example

Show the team that you trust others: your team, your colleagues, and your boss. Your team members are always watching and taking cues from you - so show them what trust in others really looks like. For example, always thanking your team members for identifying and reporting potential safety problems and following up with them to describe the outcome of the report is an excellent way to lead by example. Also, model personal accountability by sharing a story from your past about something you could have done better related to patient safety.     

##### Communicate Openly

There are several ways to get your team talking to one another in an honest, meaningful way:  Define and share the purpose of the team, as well as each person's role, and encourage each team member to ask questions, and discuss his or her expectations.

Next, conduct team-building exercises. Planned well, these exercises can help "break the ice" and encourage people to open up and start communicating. To go deeper with team building consider using psychometric instruments such as Myers-Briggs Personality Testing to help your people understand and appreciate those that they work with, and that other people's approaches and insights can be as valid as their own.

Meet regularly, so that all team members have a chance to talk about their progress, and discuss any problems that they're experiencing. This time spent face-to-face is an important part of getting to know each other, and to help one another solve problems.

##### Make it personal

Create situations that help your team members bond by sharing personal stories, and what's going on outside work. You may do this by asking sensitively about their family, or about their hobbies.
